sourceText: - **1. Monty Hall** \[Predict\]: pick a door, the host opens a goat, stay or switch? Auto-play 1,000 rounds; switching wins about 2/3.
title: A host who knows the prize
lens: the knowledgeable host protocol

sourceText: - **2. Monty Hall, 100 doors** \[Gotcha\]: the host opens 98 goat doors. Suddenly switching feels obvious, and the 3-door case clicks.
title: Ninety-eight goat doors
lens: the unchosen probability mass

sourceText: - **3. Monty Fall** \[Gotcha\]: the host trips and opens a random door that happens to show a goat. Now it really is 50/50, because the host's knowledge was doing the work.
title: The host opened a goat by accident
lens: the random-host likelihood

sourceText: - **4. Birthday paradox** \[Predict\]: guess how many people give a 50% chance of a shared birthday. Answer: 23. Slide to 70 for 99.9%.
title: Any pair shares a birthday
lens: the event of any matching pair

sourceText: - **5. Your birthday** \[Split\]: half are asked about any shared birthday, half about someone sharing *theirs*. The second needs 253 people for 50%.
title: Someone shares your birthday
lens: a specified birthday rather than any pair

sourceText: - **6. Boy or girl** \[Gotcha\]: a family has two kids, at least one a boy. Chance both are boys? 1/3, not 1/2.
title: Condition on at least one boy
lens: the family-level conditioning event

sourceText: - **7. The Tuesday boy** \[Gotcha\]: at least one is a boy born on Tuesday. The answer jumps to 13/27, and the grid of 196 cases shows why.
title: A boy in a named day category
lens: the specified reporting category

sourceText: - **8. Bertrand's box** \[Gotcha\]: three boxes (gold-gold, silver-silver, gold-silver). You draw gold; the other coin is gold with probability 2/3.
title: Gold from a mixed box
lens: the box-selection prior and gold likelihood

sourceText: - **9. Three prisoners** \[Gotcha\]: a guard names one prisoner who will die. Your survival odds don't change, but the other prisoner's double.
title: What the guard could have said
lens: the guard's announcement protocol

sourceText: - **10. Two envelopes** \[Gotcha\]: switching always seems to gain 25% in expectation. Swipe to find the broken step.
title: Assign the envelopes first
lens: the assignment probability before observing money

sourceText: - **11. Sleeping Beauty** \[Split\]: poll viewers as "halfers" or "thirders", then show each side's best argument.
title: Sample experiments or visits?
lens: the unit being sampled in repeated experiments

sourceText: - **12. Bertrand's chord** \[Slider\]: three ways to draw a "random" chord give answers of 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4. "Random" needs a definition.
title: Two ways to randomize a chord
lens: the midpoint sampling measure

sourceText: - **13. Penney's game** \[Predict\]: pick a 3-flip pattern; the app always picks one that beats it, up to 7:1.
title: A race between overlapping patterns
lens: the suffix state in first-pattern arrival

sourceText: - **14. HH vs HT** \[Predict\]: which takes more flips on average to appear? HH takes 6, HT takes 4.
title: HH and HT take different times
lens: prefix overlap in waiting times

sourceText: - **15. Nontransitive dice** \[Predict\]: pick any of Efron's dice; the app picks one that beats yours 2/3 of the time.
title: Dice can beat each other in a cycle
lens: the ordered face-pair comparison

sourceText: - **16. Parrondo's paradox** \[Slider\]: two games that each lose money win when alternated.
title: Mixing changes the capital states
lens: the stationary capital-residue distribution

sourceText: - **17. The secretary problem** \[Measure\]: swipe through 100 candidates and stop on the best. Skipping the first 37% maximizes your odds.
title: When to start accepting records
lens: the skip threshold under random ordering

sourceText: - **18. Friendship paradox** \[Gotcha\]: on average, your friends have more friends than you do. Popular people are overcounted.
title: Popular friends get sampled more
lens: size-weighted degree sampling

sourceText: - **19. Inspection paradox** \[Gotcha\]: buses come every 10 minutes on average, yet your typical wait is longer than 5. Long gaps catch more arrivals.
title: Long bus gaps catch more arrivals
lens: gap-length weighting rather than uniform gaps

sourceText: - **20. Coupon collector** \[Predict\]: how many packs to complete a 50-sticker album? About 225.
title: The last missing sticker
lens: the sum of successive collection waits

sourceText: - **21. Fake the coin** \[Measure\]: type 100 "random" H/T; the app spots you're human because you avoided long runs.
title: How many runs should a coin make?
lens: transitions in an independent sequence

sourceText: - **22. Longest streak** \[Predict\]: guess the longest run in 100 real flips. It's usually 6 or 7.
title: A bound on long heads windows
lens: overlap in a longest-run upper bound

sourceText: - **23. Gambler's fallacy** \[Measure\]: after 5 heads, call the next flip. Your hit rate stays stubbornly at 50%.
title: The coin does not owe you tails
lens: independence after a specified streak

sourceText: - **24. Hot hand bias** \[Gotcha\]: in 4-flip sequences, the average share of heads after heads is about 40%, not 50%.
title: Average the selected short sequences
lens: sequence-level averaging after heads

sourceText: - **25. Shuffle feels rigged** \[Gotcha\]: truly random playlists repeat artists, which is why music apps make shuffle *less* random.
title: Uniform shuffles allow repeats
lens: adjacent artist repeats under uniform shuffling

sourceText: - **26. Spot the random dots** \[Split\]: which pattern is random? Most pick the evenly spaced one; the clumpy one is random.
title: Random points leave empty cells
lens: gaps under independent uniform placement

sourceText: - **27. Two-dice sums** \[Predict\]: build the histogram roll by roll; 7 wins because it has the most combinations.
title: Why seven has more pairs
lens: ordered pairs behind a sum

sourceText: - **28. De Méré's bet** \[Predict\]: one six in 4 rolls (51.8%) vs double six in 24 rolls of two dice (49.1%).
title: One six or one double six?
lens: the complement over independent attempts

sourceText: - **29. Waiting for a six** \[Predict\]: it takes 6 rolls on average, yet only 66.5% of the time do you get one within 6.
title: A six within six rolls
lens: finite-horizon success versus mean waiting time

sourceText: - **30. Catch the loaded die** \[Slider\]: set the bias, roll until you're sure. Small biases need hundreds of rolls.
title: A biased die produces a count
lens: the likelihood of one specified count

sourceText: - **31. Benford's law** \[Predict\]: guess how often real-world numbers start with 1. About 30%.
title: The first digit is not uniform
lens: a logarithmic leading-digit model

sourceText: - **32. Pick a number 1–10** \[Split\]: see the crowd's distribution; 7 dominates and 1 and 10 are rare.
title: A toy crowd favors seven
lens: the group mixture behind an observed choice share

sourceText: - **33. Rock-paper-scissors bot** \[Measure\]: a simple pattern-learner beats most people over 50 rounds.
title: Exploit a predictable opponent
lens: the payoff from an assumed response probability

sourceText: - **34. Seven shuffles** \[Slider\]: it takes about 7 riffle shuffles to mix a deck well (Bayer & Diaconis, 1992).
title: An ideal ten-card riffle model
lens: one permutation's deviation from uniformity

sourceText: - **35. 52 factorial** \[Gotcha\]: a well-shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order never seen before in history.
title: Count orders on a logarithmic scale
lens: the factorial number of distinct permutations

sourceText: - **36. Stock or coin?** \[Split\]: guess which chart is a real stock and which is a coin-flip random walk.
title: A coin walk can look like a trend
lens: diffusive displacement rather than a market forecast

sourceText: - **37. Lottery 1-2-3-4-5-6** \[Gotcha\]: the same odds as any combination, but thousands play it, so a win pays less.
title: Share the winning lottery pot
lens: the number of co-winners sharing a fixed prize

sourceText: - **38. Seeds** \[Slider\]: set a pseudo-random seed and the "random" sequence repeats exactly.
title: A seed reproduces the next state
lens: a deterministic generator recurrence

sourceText: - **39. Coins have memory of their start** \[Story\]: in about 350,000 flips, coins landed on their starting side about 50.8% of the time (Bartoš et al., 2023).
title: A tiny excess over half
lens: the observed share versus the proposed coin model

sourceText: - **40. Monopoly heatmap** \[Predict\]: guess the most-landed square. Jail, thanks to the dice-and-card mechanics.
title: A toy jail-detour chain
lens: the visit rate in a stated two-state board model

sourceText: - **41. Positive mammogram** \[Predict\]: 1% prevalence, 90% sensitivity, 9% false positives. Chance of cancer after a positive? About 9%.
title: A positive result needs a base rate
lens: true and false positives in one population

sourceText: - **42. Same problem, as people** \[Split\]: half see percentages, half see "10 of 1,000 women...". The frequency half does far better.
title: The same cases as proportions
lens: the common-population denominator

sourceText: - **43. The cab problem** \[Gotcha\]: an 80%-reliable witness says the cab was blue, but only 15% of cabs are. Real chance: about 41%.
title: A witness names the rare cab
lens: the cab prevalence before the witness report

sourceText: - **44. Prosecutor's fallacy** \[Gotcha\]: "1 in a million chance of a match if innocent" is not "1 in a million chance of being innocent".
title: A rare match is not a posterior
lens: the prior odds behind a match likelihood

sourceText: - **45. Defense attorney's fallacy** \[Gotcha\]: few abusers become murderers, but among murdered women with abusive partners, the partner is the likely culprit.
title: Reverse the conditional carefully
lens: the specified population and reverse conditional

sourceText: - **46. Build a spam filter** \[Slider\]: toggle words like "free" and "invoice" and watch the spam probability update.
title: A word changes spam odds
lens: the likelihood ratio of a specified word

sourceText: - **47. Base-rate slider** \[Slider\]: keep the test fixed, slide prevalence from 0.1% to 50%, and watch a positive result's meaning flip.
title: Slide the base rate, keep the test
lens: the base rate with unchanged test characteristics

sourceText: - **48. Test twice** \[Predict\]: a second independent positive takes the posterior from 9% to about 50%.
title: Two conditionally independent positives
lens: conditional independence across repeated tests

sourceText: - **49. The 99.9% terrorist detector** \[Slider\]: screen a million travelers and nearly every alarm is an innocent person.
title: A rare target in a large crowd
lens: the prevalence behind a highly accurate alarm

sourceText: - **50. Face recognition in a stadium** \[Slider\]: even accurate matching floods police with false matches in big crowds.
title: Stadium matching and false alarms
lens: the target fraction in the screened crowd

sourceText: - **51. Librarian or farmer?** \[Gotcha\]: a shy, tidy man is still more likely a farmer, since farmers vastly outnumber librarians.
title: A description versus prior odds
lens: the occupational base rate before a description

sourceText: - **52. Draw the tree** \[Slider\]: drag branch widths in a probability tree and watch the posterior box resize.
title: Weight the two branches of the tree
lens: the prior branch widths in Bayes' rule

sourceText: - **53. What a negative test means** \[Slider\]: a negative rapid test reassures less when symptoms or local prevalence are high.
title: A negative test with a high prior
lens: the probability left after a negative result

sourceText: - **54. Three friends in Seattle** \[Predict\]: each lies 1/3 of the time; all say it's raining. With a 25% prior, the chance it's raining is about 73%.
title: Three independent reports of rain
lens: the conditional independence of witness reports

sourceText: - **55. Lie detector** \[Slider\]: set accuracy and the share of liars; most "liars" flagged among honest crowds are false alarms.
title: A lie detector in an honest crowd
lens: the share of liars before a detector alarm

sourceText: - **56. "70% chance of rain"** \[Gotcha\]: it means it rains on about 70% of days with that forecast, and that calibration can be checked.
title: Seventy percent over repeated days
lens: forecast calibration over repeated outcomes

sourceText: - **57. Which urn?** \[Predict\]: draw balls one by one and watch the posterior bar between two urns shift.
title: Which urn supplied the ball?
lens: the likelihood ratio of a specified draw

sourceText: - **58. Doping tests** \[Slider\]: with few cheaters, even a good test catches many clean athletes.
title: A doping alarm in a rare class
lens: the base rate among tested athletes

sourceText: - **59. Early pregnancy test** \[Slider\]: the meaning of a faint positive changes with how many days late you are.
title: An early test changes sensitivity
lens: the sensitivity at a stated testing time

sourceText: - **60. "Most crashes happen near home"** \[Gotcha\]: because most driving happens near home, not because home roads are dangerous.
title: Crashes need exposure denominators
lens: driving exposure rather than crash counts alone

sourceText: - **61. Galton board** \[Predict\]: drop 1,000 balls through pegs and a bell curve builds itself.
title: The peg board counts right turns
lens: binomial paths through independent pegs

sourceText: - **62. Central limit theorem** \[Slider\]: average N rolls of a weird die; as N grows, any shape turns into a bell.
title: Averages shrink their sampling spread
lens: the finite-variance averaging scale

sourceText: - **63. Height vs wealth** \[Split\]: the tallest person is under 1.5× average height; the richest is millions of times average wealth.
title: A typical value versus an extreme
lens: the effect of an extreme observation on the mean

sourceText: - **64. Goals per match** \[Predict\]: guess the share of 0–0 football games, then see the Poisson curve fit.
title: A zero-goal toy count
lens: the event-count rate in a Poisson model

sourceText: - **65. Horse kicks** \[Story\]: Prussian cavalry deaths by horse kick fit a Poisson distribution almost perfectly (Bortkiewicz, 1898).
title: Rare incidents per unit of exposure
lens: the stated Poisson rate per exposure unit

sourceText: - **66. Waiting times** \[Slider\]: set an arrival rate and watch exponential gaps: lots of short waits, a few very long.
title: Short waits and a long tail
lens: a constant-rate waiting-time model

sourceText: - **67. The memoryless bulb** \[Gotcha\]: for a bulb with exponential lifetime, having lasted 1,000 hours doesn't shorten its remaining life.
title: The age of a memoryless bulb
lens: elapsed age in exponential conditional survival

sourceText: - **68. Free throws** \[Slider\]: a 70% shooter takes 10 shots; see how often they hit 5 or fewer.
title: Ten shots from a seventy-percent shooter
lens: the complement of five-or-fewer successes

sourceText: - **69. Tries until success** \[Predict\]: with a 1-in-20 chance per try, how many tries is typical? Many need far more than 20.
title: Twenty tries is not a guarantee
lens: finite attempts for a geometric waiting process

sourceText: - **70. Zipf's law** \[Predict\]: guess the share of English text that is "the". Around 5–7%, with each next word roughly half as common.
title: Normalize a finite Zipf vocabulary
lens: the normalization of ranked frequency weights

sourceText: - **71. 80/20** \[Slider\]: tune a Pareto distribution and see what share of the top 20% owns.
title: How much does the top fifth hold?
lens: the Pareto shape behind concentration

sourceText: - **72. Fat tails** \[Gotcha\]: under a normal model, the 1987 one-day 20% crash was a 20-plus-sigma event that "should" never happen.
title: A tail observation changes the mean
lens: tail sensitivity rather than proof of a normal law

sourceText: - **73. Hidden e** \[Predict\]: add random numbers between 0 and 1 until the sum passes 1. The average count is e ≈ 2.718.
title: Uniform draws until the sum passes one
lens: the capped waiting-time survival sum

sourceText: - **74. Beta as belief** \[Slider\]: add wins and losses and watch a beta curve sharpen around a success rate.
title: Wins sharpen an explicit prior
lens: prior counts and observed coin data

sourceText: - **75. Birthday calendar** \[Story\]: real birthdays aren't uniform; US births dip on holidays and peak in September.
title: A toy calendar with fewer dates
lens: the support size of a simplified birthday model

sourceText: - **76. Mixed heights** \[Gotcha\]: men and women differ in average height, yet the combined distribution barely shows two humps.
title: Two height groups in one mean
lens: group weights without inferring histogram modality

sourceText: - **77. The Cauchy average** \[Predict\]: average more and more samples and it never settles down.
title: A Cauchy average keeps its scale
lens: the failure of finite-variance averaging assumptions

sourceText: - **78. 68–95–99.7** \[Slider\]: drag a band of ±1, 2, 3 standard deviations and watch the coverage.
title: A stated normal-coverage approximation
lens: the coverage as a band widens

sourceText: - **79. 100-year flood** \[Gotcha\]: it has about a 26% chance of hitting during a 30-year mortgage.
title: A one-percent annual flood risk
lens: independent annual risk over a mortgage horizon

sourceText: - **80. Name that distribution** \[Predict\]: see a histogram, guess which process made it: dice, waiting times, counts or wealth.
title: A process gives the count shape
lens: the mean of a specified count-generating process

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **81. Small schools** \[Gotcha\]: the smallest schools dominate both the best and the worst score lists, simply from noise.
title: Small schools have noisy proportions
lens: sample size behind extreme observed school rates

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **82. Kidney cancer map** \[Gotcha\]: rural counties have both the highest and lowest rates, because small populations swing wildly (Wainer, 2007).
title: Small counties have variable rates
lens: population exposure behind a noisy proportion

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **83. Cover jinx** \[Gotcha\]: athletes slump after magazine covers because they were featured at a lucky peak.
title: A cover follows a lucky peak
lens: selection on an extreme noisy score

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **84. Sophomore slump** \[Predict\]: simulate skill plus luck; the top rookies of year one mostly do worse in year two.
title: The next season after a rookie peak
lens: reliability in a repeat-performance model

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **85. Praise vs punishment** \[Gotcha\]: pilots improved after being yelled at for bad landings, but would have anyway.
title: Improvement after a bad landing
lens: regression without assigning a punishment effect

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **86. Galton's heights** \[Slider\]: very tall parents have tall kids, but less extreme ones.
title: An extreme parent-height score
lens: the regression coefficient in a stated height model

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **87. Margin of error** \[Slider\]: poll 100, 1,000, 10,000 people; the ±3% at 1,000 appears on its own.
title: The poll margin has a square root
lens: the standard error before applying an interval multiplier

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **88. City vs country** \[Gotcha\]: a poll of 1,000 is about as precise for a city of a million as for a country of 300 million.
title: A city poll versus a country poll
lens: the finite-population sampling fraction

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **89. Online poll** \[Split\]: show a self-selected poll beside a random sample of the same question.
title: Self-selection changes the poll mix
lens: selection weights rather than random-sampling precision

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **90. The square-root law** \[Slider\]: to halve the error, you need four times the sample.
title: Four times the sample, half the spread
lens: the square-root precision law

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **91. Lead that grows** \[Predict\]: the share of heads converges to 50%, but the gap between heads and tails count keeps growing.
title: A fraction settles while counts wander
lens: absolute random-walk displacement

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **92. 5.0 vs 4.8 stars** \[Split\]: 3 reviews at 5.0 or 2,000 at 4.8? Shrink each toward the average to see which is better.
title: Three perfect reviews or many good ones
lens: review counts in a stated shrinkage rule

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **93. Last year's best fund** \[Gotcha\]: top-performing funds mostly fall back toward average the next year.
title: Last year's top fund regresses
lens: an assumed repeat-return reliability

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **94. Treated when worst** \[Gotcha\]: patients enroll when symptoms peak, so they improve even with a useless treatment.
title: Treatment starts at a symptom peak
lens: regression before claiming treatment causation

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **95. Speed cameras** \[Gotcha\]: cameras go up after a run of crashes, so crashes fall partly by regression alone.
title: A camera follows a crash spike
lens: selection of sites after unusually high counts

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **96. Retake the test** \[Predict\]: bottom scorers improve and top scorers slip on a retake, with no teaching.
title: A retake without new teaching
lens: opposite deviations under the same repeat-score rule

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **97. Salesperson of the quarter** \[Predict\]: simulate a team of equally skilled sellers and watch "stars" rotate.
title: The sales star and next quarter
lens: the noise share behind selected top performers

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **98. How many to survey?** \[Slider\]: set the precision you want and get the sample size.
title: Choose a desired poll half-width
lens: the sample cost of tighter precision

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **99. Stratified sampling** \[Slider\]: compare random vs stratified samples of a lumpy population; stratified wobbles less.
title: Strata have explicit population weights
lens: the strata weights needed for an aggregate estimate

sourceSection: 5. Sampling, variance & regression to the mean
sourceText: - **100. The Xbox poll** \[Story\]: a heavily skewed 2012 poll of Xbox users, reweighted by demographics, forecast the US election well (Wang, Rothschild, Goel & Gelman, 2015).
title: Reweight the Xbox-like sample
lens: the target-population mixture rather than sample composition

sourceText: - **101. Is the coin fair?** \[Slider\]: flip and watch the posterior over the coin's bias narrow with each toss.
title: Learn the coin's next-head probability
lens: the Beta-Bernoulli predictive mean

sourceText: - **102. Stubborn vs open mind** \[Slider\]: set prior strength and see how much data it takes to move each belief.
title: A strong prior takes more data
lens: prior strength under identical observations

sourceText: - **103. Two skeptics converge** \[Predict\]: two people with opposite priors see the same data and end up agreeing.
title: Opposite priors see the same evidence
lens: the influence of fixed prior counts as data accumulate

sourceText: - **104. Will the sun rise?** \[Gotcha\]: Laplace's rule of succession gives (n+1)/(n+2) after n sunrises, never quite 1.
title: A success streak is not probability one
lens: Laplace smoothing of repeated successes

sourceText: - **105. German tank problem** \[Predict\]: see a few captured serial numbers and estimate how many tanks exist.
title: The largest serial is not the total
lens: the expected unseen gap beyond a sampled maximum

sourceText: - **106. Credible vs confidence** \[Split\]: the same data, two intervals, two very different meanings.
title: A posterior band uses an explicit prior
lens: posterior conditioning rather than repeated-sampling coverage

sourceText: - **107. Bayes factor** \[Slider\]: how many heads in a row before "trick coin" beats "fair coin"?
title: Heads favor a specified trick coin
lens: the likelihood ratio against a stated alternative

sourceText: - **108. Automatic Occam's razor** \[Gotcha\]: a flexible model spreads its bets, so a simple model that fits wins the evidence.
title: Evidence rewards concentrated prediction
lens: the marginal likelihood ratio of two stated models

sourceText: - **109. Bayesian average ratings** \[Slider\]: blend each product's stars with the site average, weighted by review count.
title: Blend ratings with a prior mean
lens: the relative weight of reviews and a prior pseudoreview

sourceText: - **110. "Chance B beats A"** \[Slider\]: feed in A/B conversions and watch the posterior probability that B is better.
title: B versus a uniform uncertain A
lens: the special case of a uniform comparator posterior

sourceText: - **111. Flat isn't neutral** \[Gotcha\]: a flat prior on a probability is not flat on its odds or log-odds.
title: Uniform probability is not uniform odds
lens: the nonlinear mapping from log-odds to probability

sourceText: - **112. Finding a lost plane** \[Story\]: Bayesian search theory helped locate the USS Scorpion (1968) and Air France 447's wreck (2011).
title: A search clue changes regional odds
lens: the regional prior and clue likelihood ratio

sourceText: - **113. Normal meets normal** \[Slider\]: blend a prior mean with noisy measurements and watch the posterior shift and tighten.
title: Combine normal prior and measurement
lens: the relative precisions in a normal update

sourceText: - **114. Cromwell's rule** \[Gotcha\]: give anything a prior of exactly 0 and no evidence can ever revive it.
title: A zero prior stays zero
lens: the difference between impossible and merely unlikely

sourceText: - **115. Doomsday argument** \[Split\]: poll whether it's convincing, then show the strongest objections.
title: A stated rank-sampling assumption
lens: the sampling assumption rather than a doomsday conclusion

sourceText: - **116. Next free throw** \[Predict\]: predict the next shot from the full posterior, not just the best guess.
title: Predict the next free throw
lens: posterior prediction rather than a maximum-likelihood point

sourceText: - **117. Strength of evidence** \[Slider\]: drag a likelihood ratio and see how it multiplies your prior odds.
title: Multiply odds, then convert back
lens: likelihood ratios on the odds scale

sourceText: - **118. Three heads in a row** \[Split\]: maximum likelihood says the coin always lands heads; a Bayesian disagrees.
title: Three heads with a finite prior
lens: the prior behind a prediction after a short streak

sourceText: - **119. Lindley's paradox** \[Gotcha\]: a result can be "significant" while the Bayesian evidence favors no effect.
title: A p-value alone is not a Bayes factor
lens: the prior odds in a stated Bayesian comparison

sourceText: - **120. Your hidden rating** \[Predict\]: play matches and watch an Elo or TrueSkill estimate of your skill update.
title: A toy hidden skill update
lens: the update weight after new skill evidence

sourceText: - **121. St. Petersburg game** \[Measure\]: name your price to play a game with infinite expected value. Most say under $20.
title: Cap the doubling-payoff game
lens: the distinction between capped expectation and typical payout

sourceText: - **122. Kelly betting** \[Slider\]: choose a bet fraction on a favorable coin; too high and you go broke despite your edge.
title: Bet sizing under known odds
lens: the log-growth optimum under specified odds

sourceText: - **123. The ergodicity coin** \[Predict\]: +50% on heads, −40% on tails. The average grows, yet almost every player ends near zero.
title: Positive mean, negative compound growth
lens: arithmetic versus compound return

sourceText: - **124. Why insure?** \[Slider\]: a negative-expected-value policy makes sense once the utility curve bends.
title: Insurance and curved utility
lens: wealth-relative utility curvature in a stated model

sourceText: - **125. Lottery rollover** \[Slider\]: grow the jackpot until the ticket's expected value turns positive, then add shared winners.
title: Share the rollover prize
lens: the split jackpot conditional on a shared win

sourceText: - **126. Be the banker** \[Measure\]: play a *Deal or No Deal*-style game and see your implied risk attitude.
title: An offer versus a specified gamble
lens: the probability behind the cash expectation

sourceText: - **127. Newcomb's problem** \[Split\]: one box or two? Show the poll, then both camps' arguments.
title: A predictor's observed track record
lens: the stated evidence about a predictor without resolving a decision theory

sourceText: - **128. Pascal's mugging** \[Split\]: a tiny chance of an enormous payoff; poll whether to pay, then discuss.
title: An enormous payoff times tiny odds
lens: the explicitly assumed probability-payoff product

sourceText: - **129. Mean vs median startup** \[Gotcha\]: the average outcome is great, while the typical founder gets nothing.
title: A startup mean exceeds the typical case
lens: an extreme success in a toy payoff distribution

sourceText: - **130. Gambler's ruin** \[Slider\]: set bankrolls and edge; even a fair game ruins the poorer player most of the time.
title: A small bankroll can hit zero first
lens: absorbing boundaries in a fair game

sourceText: - **131. Martingale roulette** \[Predict\]: double after every loss; simulate until the table limit or bankroll ends it.
title: The bankroll needed after losses
lens: the geometric cost of a doubling strategy

sourceText: - **132. Value of information** \[Slider\]: how much should you pay for a forecast before planning a picnic?
title: The upper value of a perfect forecast
lens: state-contingent choices under perfect information

sourceText: - **133. Selling a house** \[Slider\]: offers arrive one by one; set your threshold and see the expected price.
title: A higher threshold means more waiting
lens: the accepted-offer mean and waiting tradeoff
